lesson.title: Galaxies and Hubble's law

steps.headline: Galaxies recede at a speed proportional to their distance: Hubble's law, v = H₀d.

lead.text: Galaxy spectra are redshifted, and the redshift grows with distance. Hubble's law gives the recession speed as v = H₀d. H₀ is the Hubble constant, about 70 km/s per megaparsec (Mpc). One Mpc is 3.26 million light-years.
Light takes time to arrive. A distance of 1 Mpc is 3.26 million light-years, so light from it has travelled for 3.26 million years.

reveal.text: You were looking at Andromeda as it was millions of years ago. The farther away a galaxy is, the older the light we see.

steps.headline: How fast does a galaxy 30 Mpc away recede, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc?

workedSteps.text: Put in the numbers. The Mpc cancels.

lead.text: Same law, a farther galaxy. Remember H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: Twice the distance gives twice the speed. At 200 Mpc the same law gives double what you just found.

steps.headline: Expansion has no centre, and running the law backwards turns a speed into a distance.

lead.text: Stretch the grid evenly and every gap grows by the same factor. A galaxy twice as far gains twice as much, so observers in any galaxy see v proportional to d. Reversing the law gives d = v ÷ H₀.
A recession speed gives a distance by d = v ÷ H₀, with H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc.

reveal.text: A faster galaxy is a farther one: you have turned a measured speed into a distance.

lead.text: Different methods give H₀ between about 67 and 73 km/s per Mpc, a disagreement called the Hubble tension. Distances found from velocities inherit that uncertainty.

reveal.text: The two values predict speeds that differ by the gap in H₀ times the distance. A small disagreement in H₀ grows with distance.

lesson.orientation: Picture the scale of the universe and use Hubble's law to link velocity and distance.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Dots A, B and C lie in a line on a rubber sheet. B is 10 cm from A and C is 20 cm from A. The sheet is stretched evenly until every gap has doubled.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a galaxy's redshift into a distance with Hubble's law and say why expansion has no centre.

recap.keyIdea: Galaxies recede at v = H₀d, so a redshift gives a distance. Uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy, so it has no centre.

blocks.text: You found that on a stretching sheet the longer gap gains twice as much, that a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at 7,000 km/s, and that one receding at 14,000 km/s is 200 Mpc away.

recap.nextHook: If everything is moving apart, it was once together. How long ago, and what afterglow would it leave?

questions.prompt: The Andromeda galaxy is about 0.78 Mpc away, and 1 Mpc = 3.26 million light-years. How long ago, in millions of years, did the light we see from it set out? Give one decimal place.
hints: A light-year is the distance light covers in one year.
Convert megaparsecs to millions of light-years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.78 × 3.26 = 2.54 million light-years, so the light left about 2.5 million years ago.

questions.onCorrect: 2.5 million years. A distance in light-years is also the light's travel time in years.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance in Mpc. Convert it to millions of light-years first.
That is the conversion for one Mpc. Andromeda is a fraction of that distance.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find the recession velocity of a galaxy 100 Mpc away, in km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 7,000 km/s. Hubble's law multiplies H₀ by the distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides H₀ by the distance. Hubble's law multiplies them.
That adds H₀ and the distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A galaxy recedes at 14,000 km/s. With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, how far away is it, in Mpc?
questions.onCorrect: 200 Mpc. Distance is the recession speed divided by H₀.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. To find the distance, divide the speed by H₀.
That divides H₀ by the speed, the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: Estimates of H₀ range from 67 to 73 km/s per Mpc. For a galaxy 300 Mpc away, by how many km/s do the two predicted velocities differ?
hints: Compute each velocity with v = H₀d, or work with the difference directly.
questions.onCorrect: 1,800 km/s. The difference in H₀ times the distance gives the difference in speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the difference in H₀. Multiply it by the distance.
That is one of the two speeds. The question asks for the difference between them.

questions.prompt: A galaxy's 500.0 nm line is observed at 510.0 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, and H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, find its distance in Mpc, to the nearest whole number.
hints: First turn the redshift into a velocity.
Then divide that velocity by H₀.
questions.onCorrect: 86 Mpc. Turn the redshift into a speed first, then divide by H₀.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed in km/s. Divide it by H₀ to get the distance.

questions.prompt: Every distant galaxy appears to recede from the Milky Way. What does this tell us about our position?
hints: Imagine standing on a different galaxy on the stretching grid.

acceptedIdeas: Nothing special: uniform expansion gives every galaxy the same view
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In a uniform expansion all spacings grow by the same factor, so observers in any galaxy see v ∝ d. Recession in every direction does not single out a centre.

choices.label: Nothing special: uniform expansion gives every galaxy the same view
The Milky Way is at the centre of the expansion
The Milky Way is the oldest galaxy

questions.onCorrect: Nothing special: uniform expansion looks the same from every galaxy.

misconceptions.feedback: If the expansion were centred on us, observers elsewhere would see something different. Check what they would see.
Recession does not say how old a galaxy is. Think about what observers in other galaxies would see.

questions.prompt: How many times farther does C move away from A than B does?
hints: How much does B's gap grow when it doubles?
How much does C's gap grow?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: B's gap grows by 10 cm and C's gap by 20 cm, so C moves twice as far.

questions.onCorrect: 2 times. Each gap grows by its own length, so longer gaps gain more: speed rises with distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That would hold if both dots slid along together. Here every gap doubles, so a longer gap gains more.
That squares the ratio. Each gap simply doubles, so each gains its own length.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is twice as far away as another. How do their recession speeds compare?
hints: Look at how v depends on d in v = H₀d.

acceptedIdeas: The farther one recedes twice as fast
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The farther one recedes twice as fast

choices.label: The farther one recedes twice as fast
They recede at the same speed
The farther one recedes half as fast

questions.onCorrect: Speed is proportional to distance, so twice the distance means twice the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed depends on distance in Hubble's law, so different distances give different speeds.
Speed grows with distance. A farther galaxy recedes faster.

hints: Write H₀ with its units, then multiply by d.

acceptedIdeas: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.

choices.label: H₀ is in km/s per Mpc, so multiplying by Mpc leaves km/s.
Because Mpc is a small unit.

questions.onCorrect: km/s per Mpc times Mpc leaves km/s, which is the unit of a speed.

misconceptions.feedback: A megaparsec is a very large unit. The cancelling comes from how H₀ is written.
Speeds have units. Here the units come from H₀ itself.

questions.prompt: Observers in another galaxy look out at the rest. What do they see?
hints: Imagine standing on a different dot of the stretching grid.

acceptedIdeas: The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance

choices.label: The same pattern: others receding, faster with distance

questions.onCorrect: On an evenly stretching grid every dot sees the same pattern, so no dot is the centre.

misconceptions.feedback: Gaps grow everywhere on the grid, so nothing stands still relative to anything.
Every gap grows, so other galaxies recede, not approach.

questions.prompt: With H₀ = 72 km/s per Mpc, find the recession speed of a galaxy 150 Mpc away, in km/s.
questions.onCorrect: 10,800 km/s. Speed is H₀ times distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides H₀ by the distance. Hubble's law multiplies them.
That adds H₀ and the distance. Multiply them.
